    Topic 9: Ownership hands-on review

    By the end, you will be able to

    • Trace owners and drops through nested scopes.
    • Repair a move error and explain the ownership transfer.
    • Choose copying, moving, or cloning for a stated requirement.
    • Complete and run a small program without relying on answer choices.
    • Read and update a sub-slice through borrowed iteration.
    • Return a borrowed word without cloning its text.
    • Combine borrowed processing with a final ownership-consuming step.

    Prerequisites: Values and scope, Moves, Copy and Clone, Shared borrowing, Mutable borrowing, Collections and iterators, and Slices. This final module topic practices selected skills from Topics 2.1–2.7. Lifetime annotations are outside this practice set. Attempt each task before consulting the solution. Allow about 90–120 minutes including the advanced exercise.

    1. Explain the terms in your own words

    Learn this in Topic 1: Values and scope, Topic 2: Moves, and Topic 3: Copy and Clone.

    For each term, give a definition and point to a concrete line in one of the exercises: value, binding, owner, scope, drop, stack, heap, move, Copy, Clone. Explain why a String binding leaving scope does not always drop its original string data: ownership may already have moved elsewhere.

    Reminder: bindings and data

    A String owns heap-backed text. Moving it transfers ownership without duplicating that text. Scope determines when a remaining owner is dropped.

    2. Trace ownership before compiling

    Learn this in Topic 1: Values and scope, Topic 2: Moves, and Topic 3: Copy and Clone.

    fn main() {
    let count = 3_u32;
    let other_count = count;
    let first = String::from("Read");
    {
        let second = first;
        let third = second.clone();
        println!("{second} {third} {count} {other_count}");
    }
}

    Write a table with one row after each let: usable bindings, current owners, and whether an independent heap allocation was created. Then predict which owned strings are dropped at the inner closing brace. Compile to check your predicted output, and explain why output alone cannot prove your ownership table.

    Solution: trace ownership

    Each row describes the state immediately after that let. Here, A and B label two independent heap allocations holding the text Read.

    After statement Usable bindings String owners New independent heap allocation?
    let count = 3_u32; count None No, u32 needs no heap allocation
    let other_count = count; count, other_count None No, the integer is copied
    let first = String::from("Read"); count, other_count, first first owns A Yes, A
    let second = first; count, other_count, second second owns A No, ownership moves from first
    let third = second.clone(); count, other_count, second, third second owns A, third owns B Yes, B contains a copy of A's text

    first is unusable after the move into second. The two integers remain usable because u32 implements Copy.

    At the inner closing brace, third is dropped first, then second, in reverse declaration order. Their drops release B and A respectively. Afterward, only count and other_count remain usable. At the outer closing brace, first does not drop A again because it has been moved from.

    Expected output:

    Read Read 3 3

    Output confirms the printed values, but it does not show which binding owns an allocation or when that allocation is released. Independent strings can print identical text. The ownership table follows from Rust's move, Copy, Clone, and scope rules.

    3. Diagnose and repair a move

    Learn this in Topic 2: Moves, with Topic 5: Mutable borrowing for the alternative solution.

    fn decorate(mut title: String) -> String {
    title.push('!');
    title
}

fn main() {
    let title = String::from("Read");
    let updated = decorate(title);
    println!("{title}");
}

    Save this in a temporary Rust file and compile it. Identify the move site and the invalid later use. Repair it without cloning: keep the returned value and print Read!. Explain who owns the string inside decorate and after its return. Do not replace the function with a borrowed API for this exercise.

    Solution: repair the move

    decorate(title) moves the string from main into the function's title parameter. The later println!("{title}") tries to use the moved binding, so the compiler reports E0382: borrow of moved value.

    Print updated, which owns the returned string:

    fn decorate(mut title: String) -> String {
    title.push('!');
    title
}

fn main() {
    let title = String::from("Read");
    let updated = decorate(title);
    println!("{updated}");
}

    Expected output:

    Read!

    Inside decorate, its title parameter owns the string. mut allows the function to append !. The final expression title moves ownership back to the caller, where updated becomes the owner. The string is dropped when updated leaves scope at the end of main.

    No clone is needed because the exercise requires only the updated string, with no independent copy of the original.

    Alternative solution: mutable borrowing

    This version explores a borrowed API. Use the first solution to complete Exercise 3's requirement to practice ownership transfer.

    fn decorate(title: &mut String) {
    title.push('!');
}

fn main() {
    let mut title = String::from("Read");
    decorate(&mut title);
    println!("{title}");
}

    Expected output:

    Read!

    main keeps ownership of the string. &mut title lends exclusive access to decorate, whose &mut String parameter lets it modify the caller's string. The binding in main needs mut to allow this mutable borrow. After the call, main can use title again. No returned string or clone is needed, and the string is dropped at the end of main.

    For more practice, see Mutable borrowing.

    4. Complete the snapshot program

    Learn this in Topic 2: Moves and Topic 3: Copy and Clone.

    The requirement is different here: preserve the original title while changing a second independently owned title. Complete the starter in examples/02-ownership-and-borrowing/09-hands-on/starter.rs.

    fn decorate(title: String) -> String {
    todo!("Return the owned title with an exclamation mark appended")
}

fn main() {
    let original = String::from("Read Rust");
    // TODO: Make an independent snapshot before transferring original.
    let snapshot: String = todo!("Choose an explicit ownership operation");
    let updated = decorate(original);
    assert_eq!(snapshot, "Read Rust");
    assert_eq!(updated, "Read Rust!");
    println!("snapshot: {snapshot}, updated: {updated}");
}

    From the repository root:

    rustc examples/02-ownership-and-borrowing/09-hands-on/starter.rs -o /tmp/rust-ownership-practice
/tmp/rust-ownership-practice

    The starter deliberately panics at todo!() until completed. Success means both assertions pass and the output is:

    snapshot: Read Rust, updated: Read Rust!

    Explain why a clone is justified by this requirement but unnecessary in Exercise 3. Then add an empty-title case: its snapshot must remain empty and its decorated result must be !.

    Solution: preserve an independent snapshot

    Clone the original before moving it into decorate. The snapshot keeps its own text while the function changes the string it receives.

    fn decorate(mut title: String) -> String {
    title.push('!');
    title
}

fn main() {
    let original = String::from("Read Rust");
    let snapshot = original.clone();
    let updated = decorate(original);
    assert_eq!(snapshot, "Read Rust");
    assert_eq!(updated, "Read Rust!");
    println!("snapshot: {snapshot}, updated: {updated}");

    let original = String::new();
    let snapshot = original.clone();
    let updated = decorate(original);
    assert_eq!(snapshot, "");
    assert_eq!(updated, "!");
}

    decorate owns its title, appends !, and returns ownership to updated. The assertions check that the snapshot stays unchanged and the updated string contains the added punctuation, including for an empty title. The empty-title checks produce no additional output.

    Unlike Exercise 3, this requirement needs two independently owned strings, so the clone is justified.

    5. Iterate over a selected slice

    Learn this in Topic 5: Mutable borrowing, Topic 6: Collections and iterators, and Topic 7: Slices.

    A slice lets a function work on just the selected elements while the caller keeps the whole collection. The range 1..3 includes indices 1 and 2.

    Complete these functions without cloning or consuming the vector:

    fn sum_values(values: &[i32]) -> i32 {
    todo!("Use a for loop with iter() to sum the values")
}

fn add_one_to_each(values: &mut [i32]) {
    todo!("Use iter_mut() to increase each selected value by one")
}

fn main() {
    let mut numbers = vec![10, 20, 30, 40];
    let total = sum_values(&numbers[1..3]);
    assert_eq!(total, 50);
    add_one_to_each(&mut numbers[1..3]);
    assert_eq!(numbers, vec![10, 21, 31, 40]);
    println!("middle sum: {total}");
    println!("updated: {numbers:?}");
}

    Save your attempt in a temporary .rs file and run it with rustc, as in Exercise 4. Then check both functions with a whole array and an empty slice: an empty sum must be 0, and updating an empty slice must do nothing. Use small numbers so addition stays within i32 limits.

    Explain why *value is needed to update an element, why indices 0 and 3 remain unchanged, and why numbers remains usable after both calls. What would happen if you tried &numbers[1..5] with this four-element vector?

    Solution: shared and mutable iteration 
    fn sum_values(values: &[i32]) -> i32 {
    let mut total = 0;
    for value in values.iter() {
        total += *value;
    }
    total
}

fn add_one_to_each(values: &mut [i32]) {
    for value in values.iter_mut() {
        *value += 1;
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut numbers = vec![10, 20, 30, 40];
    let total = sum_values(&numbers[1..3]);
    assert_eq!(total, 50);
    add_one_to_each(&mut numbers[1..3]);
    assert_eq!(numbers, vec![10, 21, 31, 40]);
    println!("middle sum: {total}");
    println!("updated: {numbers:?}");

    let mut array = [1, 2];
    assert_eq!(sum_values(&array), 3);
    add_one_to_each(&mut array);
    assert_eq!(array, [2, 3]);

    let mut empty: [i32; 0] = [];
    assert_eq!(sum_values(&empty), 0);
    add_one_to_each(&mut empty);
    assert_eq!(empty, []);
}

    iter() yields &i32; dereferencing reads the integer for the sum. iter_mut() yields &mut i32; *value += 1 changes the original element. Both functions borrow, so numbers keeps ownership. Only indices 1 and 2 are included in the mutable slice. Its borrow ends before the vector is read again. An out-of-bounds range such as 1..5 would panic.

    Expected output:

    middle sum: 50
updated: [10, 21, 31, 40]

    After updating &mut numbers[1..3], which elements changed?




    6. Return a borrowed word

    Learn this in Topic 4: Shared borrowing and Topic 7: Slices and text APIs.

    A text slice views existing UTF-8 text. Return the first whitespace-separated word without allocating a new String. Use the split_whitespace() iterator from Topic 7: next() selects its first item, and unwrap_or("") supplies an empty result when there is no word.

    fn first_word(text: &str) -> &str {
    todo!("Return the first word, or an empty slice when there is none")
}

fn main() {
    let sentence = String::from("Rust makes borrowing useful");
    let word = first_word(&sentence);
    assert_eq!(word, "Rust");
    println!("first word: {word}");
    println!("still owned: {sentence}");
}

    Run your completed program, then add assertions for "hello", "", whitespace-only text, and " café Rust". Expected results are "hello", "", "", and "café". Explain who owns the returned word's text.

    Text range indices count bytes. An arbitrary byte boundary can split a UTF-8 character and cause a panic; splitting on whitespace returns valid text slices. Try inserting sentence.clear() before printing word, read the compiler error, then move the mutation after the last use of word and run again.

    Solution: borrow from the input text 
    fn first_word(text: &str) -> &str {
    text.split_whitespace().next().unwrap_or("")
}

fn main() {
    let sentence = String::from("Rust makes borrowing useful");
    let word = first_word(&sentence);
    assert_eq!(word, "Rust");
    println!("first word: {word}");
    println!("still owned: {sentence}");

    assert_eq!(first_word("hello"), "hello");
    assert_eq!(first_word(""), "");
    assert_eq!(first_word(" \t\n"), "");
    assert_eq!(first_word("  café Rust"), "café");
}

    The result for a nonempty word points into the input text; no word is cloned. sentence continues to own its text. The returned reference must stay valid while used, so clearing sentence before the last use of word is rejected. After that last use, the borrow can end and clearing the string is allowed.

    Expected output:

    first word: Rust
still owned: Rust makes borrowing useful

    Why is clearing sentence before a later use of word rejected?

    7. Advanced: borrow, update, then consume titles

    Learn this in Topic 2: Moves, Topic 5: Mutable borrowing, Topic 6: Collections and iterators, and Topic 7: Slice APIs.

    Combine three access patterns in one pipeline: borrow to read, borrow mutably to edit, then take ownership to select strings for a new collection.

    • Implement mark_titles with iter_mut() to append ! to each selected title.
    • Implement total_bytes with iter() to sum the selected strings' byte lengths.
    • Implement keep_long_titles with into_iter() to consume the input vector and move titles of at least minimum_bytes into a new vector, in input order.
    • Use no clone() or to_string(). Count bytes with len(), not characters: "café" has five UTF-8 bytes and four characters.

    Complete this starter:

    fn mark_titles(titles: &mut [String]) {
    todo!("Append ! through mutable references")
}

fn total_bytes(titles: &[String]) -> usize {
    todo!("Sum byte lengths through shared references")
}

fn keep_long_titles(titles: Vec<String>, minimum_bytes: usize) -> Vec<String> {
    todo!("Move matching strings into a new Vec")
}

fn main() {
    let mut titles = vec![
        String::from("Read"),
        String::from("Code"),
        String::from("Test"),
        String::from("Go"),
    ];
    mark_titles(&mut titles[1..3]);
    assert_eq!(titles, ["Read", "Code!", "Test!", "Go"]);
    let bytes = total_bytes(&titles[1..3]);
    assert_eq!(bytes, 10);
    println!("selected bytes: {bytes}");
    println!("before move: {titles:?}");

    let kept = keep_long_titles(titles, 5);
    assert_eq!(kept, ["Code!", "Test!"]);
    println!("kept: {kept:?}");
}

    Add assertions for empty input, no matches, a zero threshold, and a title containing "café". Predict which strings are dropped during selection and which survive in kept. Then try printing titles after the final call, explain the compiler error, and remove that invalid print.

    Solution: combine all three iterator modes 
    fn mark_titles(titles: &mut [String]) {
    for title in titles.iter_mut() {
        title.push('!');
    }
}

fn total_bytes(titles: &[String]) -> usize {
    let mut total = 0;
    for title in titles.iter() {
        total += title.len();
    }
    total
}

fn keep_long_titles(titles: Vec<String>, minimum_bytes: usize) -> Vec<String> {
    let mut kept = Vec::new();
    for title in titles.into_iter() {
        if title.len() >= minimum_bytes {
            kept.push(title);
        }
    }
    kept
}

fn main() {
    let mut titles = vec![
        String::from("Read"),
        String::from("Code"),
        String::from("Test"),
        String::from("Go"),
    ];
    mark_titles(&mut titles[1..3]);
    assert_eq!(titles, ["Read", "Code!", "Test!", "Go"]);
    let bytes = total_bytes(&titles[1..3]);
    assert_eq!(bytes, 10);
    println!("selected bytes: {bytes}");
    println!("before move: {titles:?}");

    let kept = keep_long_titles(titles, 5);
    assert_eq!(kept, ["Code!", "Test!"]);
    println!("kept: {kept:?}");

    let mut empty: Vec<String> = Vec::new();
    mark_titles(&mut empty);
    assert_eq!(total_bytes(&empty), 0);
    assert!(keep_long_titles(empty, 5).is_empty());
    assert!(keep_long_titles(vec![String::from("Go")], 5).is_empty());
    assert_eq!(keep_long_titles(vec![String::new()], 0), [""]);
    let unicode = vec![String::from("café")];
    assert_eq!(total_bytes(&unicode), 5);
    assert_eq!(keep_long_titles(unicode, 5), ["café"]);
}

    The first two functions borrow slices, so the caller retains its vector. keep_long_titles takes ownership of the vector and into_iter() yields owned strings. push(title) moves each matching string into kept. Rejected strings are dropped at the end of their loop iteration. Kept strings are dropped when the returned vector is dropped.

    The original titles binding is unusable after the consuming call. A new vector may allocate storage for its elements, but no string text is cloned.

    Expected output:

    selected bytes: 10
before move: ["Read", "Code!", "Test!", "Go"]
kept: ["Code!", "Test!"]

    Reference and completion criteria

    After your attempt, compare with solution.rs in the same example folder. For Exercise 2, first becomes unusable when moved into second; cloning creates the independently owned third. Both are dropped in the inner scope. For Exercise 3, print updated instead of the moved title.

    You are ready to continue when you can complete the code, explain every ownership transfer, justify the snapshot clone, and describe the compiler error without consulting the solution. Revisit the linked prerequisite for any term you cannot explain. Also demonstrate that your slice functions accept arrays, vectors, and empty slices, and explain why a borrowed word cannot outlive its input. This set practices selected skills from Topics 1–7, not the whole module. For the advanced exercise, explain why the first two calls preserve the caller's vector and the third consumes it, and trace ownership of kept and rejected titles.

    Next: continue the learning path with Shared borrowing, or proceed to Module 3 if you have already completed the remaining Module 2 foundations.
